utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: A very good afternoon to everybody. Please be seated. May we hear the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And the appearances, please, for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Joanna Korner, Nicholas Koumjian, assisted by Ruth Karper, case manager. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Also the Defence team in the entire composition.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, good afternoon. Branko Lukic, John Ostojic, and Danilo Cirkovic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We have a number of difficult issues on the agenda. May I first announce two things: As to the character of the issues to be discussed today, this is an ongoing hearing today and not a Status Conference. And secondly, you may have heard on the corridors that the President of this Tribunal has decided that the plenary would not take place as envisaged the 2nd and 3rd of March, but 11, 12, and 13 December -- sorry. It should read December also, 2nd, 3rd December in the transcript. But we can't follow these in and out decisions. And therefore, this Trial Chamber has decided to continue. I know, and we are all aware, that we still have to decide on the motion on mistrial. But in principle, to proceed as envisaged in the entire week of December until, in case we proceed, the ten witnesses are -- not the witnesses are exhausted, but the list of witnesses is exhausted. So as already indicated last Friday, let us please start, for reasons we just discussed, with the list of witnesses that should be concluded today. Then we have on our agenda for today the motion on mistrial. Then we have to discuss the question of experts. And then maybe in this order, the question whether or not the Defence has lived up to their obligation under Rule 65 ter (g), and in case if not, we expect submissions by the parties on possible reactions to this fact. But let us please start, and I think it seems to be a relatively short exercise, with the finalisation of the list of witnesses. As already indicated, only those witnesses will stay on the list, on the so-called final witness list, where it can be demonstrated today that the expected testimony is not irrelevant or repetitive. May we start with the first one, which in my list, should be number 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Are we in private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And may I ask the Defence, we received the two motions to summarise the motions. Please, Mr. Ostojic, the floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, Your Honours. We have filed with the Court two motion which are the initial motion, then the supplement as requested and as we envisioned in connection with the motion for mistrial. It is a difficult motion to present on behalf of the Defence because quite frankly the Defence from the outset has felt that we have worked well with the OTP, and now in hindsight, quite frankly, we believe that we have been misled and betrayed by the OTP. Specifically I believe that this Court is required to examine as highlighted in our motion and to determine what is the standard for which a mistrial can and should be granted. The rules do not envision, and do not give us those factors. I would suggest to the Court that one or more of the following four certainly warrants that a mistrial be granted. One, if there is a willful withholding of relevant information which would impede justice. Two, intentionally concealing evidence which would otherwise ensure a fair trial. Three, knowingly and selectively presenting evidence which is tainted, spoiled, or misleading. And four, deliberate omissions when confronted not only by the Defence but by this Trial Chamber of critical issues that are brought before the Court through the various witnesses. In the instant case, I was quite surprised that the OTP continues to be indifferent and callous in its approach to the misdeeds that they have committed. Last week on the 21st of November, they clearly state that they recognise and acknowledge that the production of those Rule 68 documents should have been produced as the decisional authority dictates in a timely and proper manner, meaning that they should have been disclosed well before the start of this trial; at the very least, during the trial. But most certainly before the Rule 98 bis motions were filed. To claim, as the OTP does, that "in their opinion certain witnesses were less than credible" is neither comical nor a tragic comedy but it is in our opinion a mockery of the Defence, a mockery of the justice system, and a mockery of the Tribunal. It is not for the OTP to decide, I say respectfully to them, which witnesses may or may not be credible. It is for this Court to decide that. It is for the accused through his counsel to test the veracity of each witness presented by the OTP. We submit that the OTP has not only violated one of the foregoing four bases for a mistrial, but in fact all four. They have been willfully withholding evidence. They have been intentionally concealing such evidence. They have knowingly and selectively presented evidence which in our opinion is tainted, and they have made deliberate omissions. We the Defence do not pass judgement on the OTP's ethics or their procedural missteps. We however request this Trial Chamber to tell us what is it that constitutes a fair trial, and therefore we request that Dr. Stakic be given that fair trial. We therefore respectfully request that the OTP's attempt to apologise and to minimise the effect of their transgressions is simply placing a bandage on a mortal wound. The OTP admits that its disclosure was not prompt. It admits that its disclosure was note proper, to both the statements as well as the exhibits that should have been proffered earlier. We believe respectfully that the next question the Court should examine, after examining what are the standards that dictate and warrant that a mistrial be given, and is that is what is the prejudice suffered by the accused? The prejudice we believe, as the OTP very well knows, is obvious. The OTP knows and the Defence has from the outset of this case insisted that the accused get a fair trial. That is the fundamental prejudice that has been deprived and denied Dr. Stakic. Dr. Stakic also has other fundamental rights that are guaranteed by this Tribunal that this Chamber must protect. That is, that he has a right to confront through his counsel people who make accusations against him. He has a direct right to cross-examine witnesses. We have been deprived of that right by virtue of these late, untimely, and incomplete disclosures. Dr. Stakic also has a right to remain silent. Another right that obviously, because of these late disclosures, he has been deprived. As cited in the decisional authority in our brief, namely OTP versus Furundzija and OTP versus Delalic, the Defence submits that we were deprived of our right to adequately prepare our Defence, deprived the right to have data that would assist us in the preparation not only in the cross-examination of OTP witnesses, but have been deprived the right to prepare witnesses which we expect to bring in the Defence case in chief. Several examples of the OTP's transgressions perhaps may highlight the severity of that which they have done. Some in the past and certainly these now in the present. And I say with confidence, since this morning we received yet another Rule 68 statement and documents, that there will be those transgressions in the future. But to highlight for the Court how we have been prejudiced, the past, by way of example, one witness, their purported military expert, took the stand. Gave the solemn declaration. Proceeded to tell this Court and insisted to tell this Court that he was objective. During, not before, during his testimony, the Defence received in excess of 90 exhibits, all military related exhibits, that this witness never even reviewed. And we're speaking of Mr. Ewan Brown. How can the Defence prepare to cross-examine a witness or to even argue that his credibility should not be accepted by this Court if, upon his insistence, he claims he's objective, believes he's objective, yet the OTP refused, as I stated earlier intentionally, knowingly, and deliberately concealed material which is relevant in their opinion and the opinion of the Defence, and since the Court admitted those documents, in the opinion of the Chamber as well. We were deprived to have an opportunity to review that material, deprived to have an opportunity to cross-examine this witness on those 90-plus documents. That was their past transgression. The OTP at that time also stated that they felt bad, and that they were sorry. No Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. sanction imposed; a warning to produce all such documents as required under the rules. The OTP continues in its indifference, and now in the present, if we take a look at the documents that they have produced to you, it is not a question of the five or so individuals that were members of the Crisis Staff, our highlights 30 witnesses who contradict, who rebut the testimony of the witnesses that they called in their case in chief. It is those 30 witnesses that also cause us concern. However, to highlight the present transgression, they take a statement of Slobodan Kuruzovic. At what time? After the testimony of Witness Q? Hardly. Well before. They, in fact, question Mr. Kuruzovic about the testimony given by Witness Q. They question him on issues, since they had her statement prior to her testimony, they don't offer that to the Defence because they themselves have deemed it to be one of two things: Irrelevant or not credible. Rule 68 envisions three specific purposes for which the OTP is mandatorily required to produce statements, documents, and other evidence to the Defence. Those three reasons, as I'm sure the Court knows, are the innocence of the accused. If they are in possession of evidence which would show the innocence of the accused, they should produce it. When, not when it dawns on them to produce it. As soon as possible or as soon as practicable. They have done neither. The second option that they have in which they are required to produce evidence is if there is any evidence to mitigate, mitigate, the guilt of the accused. Likewise, they failed to do that and did not meet their obligation. Third, and I must highlight it because I used it in the example of the present transgressions, they are compelled and required to produce evidence which would or may attack the credibility of any witnesses or evidence that they present. The most classic case would be Witness Q testifying about crimes that have occurred personally to her. The OTP having Mr. Kuruzovic's statements and not providing that to us. We were asked by this Trial Chamber whether or not we would cross-examine Witness Q on the crimes that she has sustained. And we told the Court at that time truthfully "we don't have evidence that would assist us to determine whether or not she is credible or not on that issue." Specifically, a discussion was held on that, and the OTP represented to the Court that they believed she is credible, meaning that they didn't have any evidence to suggest any contrary indication. Yet, throughout the entire period, they continued to have Mr. Kuruzovic's testimony, which is obviously contradictory to what Witness Q has said. I can't tell the Court, nor no one can envision what the future transgressions will be. But the Defence certainly, as I started in the opening remarks, feel most definitely betrayed. The Defence jointly has made representations to Dr. Stakic, and we have told him that the Tribunal will treat him fairly and that his fundamental rights will be secured. We continue to tell Dr. Stakic, throughout the proceedings, that the OTP is acting in a manner with great professionalism and honour and dignity. I retract those statements that I made to Dr. Stakic about the OTP. Dr. Stakic was misrepresented by the Defence. The Defence assured Dr. Stakic that he would be given a fair trial. We believed that all the documents were presented to us, at the very least, those critical documents which go to specific ingredients of each of the eight counts in the fourth amended complaint. We insisted that Dr. Stakic waive his right to have a new trial when asked by the Court under the circumstances that presented itself. We were wrong. Dr. Stakic, I believe, has a right to revoke and has a right to restate his position based upon these current events, based upon these current transgressions by the OTP. And we believe he should be given that right. Dr. Stakic relied on his detriment when we represented to him that he would get a fair trial. We were simply wrong. It is neither fair nor does it promote justice when either party conceals evidence, specifically evidence which the Court had requested time and time again. We discussed things as the Court recalls, Mr. Baltic and the evidence of possibly Mr. Halilovic and Dr. Plavsic. The OTP stood silent. Was this Court asking them to bring witnesses other than members of the Crisis Staff? Was this Court not clear enough that they requested witnesses who were precise and concrete on the fundamental issues necessary to render a decision? The OTP sat silent, indifferent during the entire time knowingly concealing the evidence which the Court requested, which the Defence demanded, which it never received. Interestingly enough, during our summer pause, the OTP again proceeded on a mission, and they took another statement of a witness at which point, despite the fact that the parties were arguing over various things, various disclosures, the OTP sat on its hands again. The rule specifically states and is very clear that they must advise us and tell us about the evidence. Their simple excuse that there was a translation delay or a problem in translating the tape is not an excuse that should be accepted in any Court, much less this Tribunal. At the very least, we would have expected, and at the very least the rules require, and they use the word "shall" mandatorily require the OTP to either tell us verbally or in writing that they are in possession of such evidence and at that time that may be convenient or as soon as practicable they will produce that to us. They have done neither. They failed in their obligation. The Defence has failed to read the OTP's strategy and gamesmanship in advising Dr. Stakic. A fair trial has not been given to date. A fair trial by proceeding in my opinion will not be given to Dr. Stakic. And we demand respectfully from this Court that you examine those five disclosures that they have presented, not the five witnesses from the Crisis Staff, but the five independent disclosures and determine whether or not there was a breach and extent of the prejudice to Dr. Stakic. Finally, if I may add, the OTP has called many what they coin "in-house witnesses." We heard from Mr. Inayat twice. We have given him, and we are very flexible, although he has prepared for many years on this case since he was the team leader, et cetera, we asked them directly about Rule 68. Team leader, criminal investigator, wealth of experience, took the solemn declaration, sat silently. Could have easily got up. Could have easily discussed it with Mr. Koumjian or anyone at the OTP based upon what the Court's inquiring, based upon the order that the Court gave on that date that we should comply at the very least with giving the Defence notification of the statements and witnesses of the members of the Crisis Staff in our possession. Instead, they merely continued to flood this Chamber with in-house witnesses. They refused to comply with the rules, but demand and insist that the Defence at all times be prompt and ready to proceed. I believe the Defence was ready and did proceed at each and every occasion, and we believe that we did cross-examine the witnesses to the extent available to us. However, and unfortunately, that was not enough. The fact that we cross-examined witnesses does not absolve their transgressions and does not and cannot mitigate in any way the rights of Dr. Stakic. He had a right, as all accused do in this Tribunal, to the presumption of innocence. He had a right to a fair trial. He had a right to confront the witnesses that the OTP brings against him. All those rights were denied by virtue of their conduct. We respectfully request that the Trial Chamber grants our motion for a mistrial and that this trial, although I recognise that judicial economy may weigh against restarting it, I am confident that many of the witnesses that the OTP has called they will probably not call again. I think that we cannot look at economy to make a decision if a man's fundamental rights and his right to freedom can ever be outweighed. And as it is this Trial Chamber's unfortunate duty to have to make this ruling, we insist and believe not only has there been a transgression that has been admitted to, it is severe and constitutes and warrants a mistrial, but also there has been severe prejudice suffered by Dr. Stakic. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this additional oral explanation of the two motions we have before us. Only to be clear, for the record, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to be decided is only the request following paragraph 44 of the Defence motion of November 15, 2002, under (a), because unanimously the other points, (b) to (e), were declared moot. But I think to a certain extent, they are included in this main request to order mistrial. So therefore, the submission and the response by the Prosecution should be limited to this number -- to this letter (a) of the motion. And finally, just that the transcript reads correct, I think you wanted to say in page 18, line 1, the fourth amended indictment where as it reads as you stated first amended complaint. This should be corrected. Thank you. Please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have sat and listened to many insulting speeches in the course of my career. But I don't think I've ever listened to one quite as vulgar, quite as insulting as that just made by Mr. Ostojic. Without one iota of grounds for alleging that myself and Mr. Koumjian and anyone else involved in the OTP have adopted an indifferent and callous willfully concealing and gamesmanship are the other adjectives that he employs. Your Honour, everything that he has said today could have been said without these unnecessary allegations of misconduct. Your Honour, I am not going to go through what I said to Your Honour last week when Mr. Ostojic couldn't be bothered to come and support his own motion clearly written by him and unknown or unsupported by Mr. Lukic who was unable to explain what should happen. When I gave a long list of the reasons and the number of documents that we had gone through in order to try and comply with Rule 68. And without, of course, as Your Honour knows, a scintilla of assistance from the Defence as to what it was they wanted us to look for. Your Honour, all I want to say is this: In this lengthy hyperbole from Mr. Ostojic, he hasn't actually pointed to one iota of prejudice that has been caused to Dr. Stakic. What is it he says that he would have asked the various witnesses who he has listed who referred in passing to some of these people that were interviewed had he had the Rule 68? Your Honour, the remedy, and we have always accepted it was an oversight. It was unfortunate. But it was not done deliberately or with malice or any of the phrases used by Mr. Ostojic. The remedy is a simple one, not one of mistrial. Is that if Mr. Ostojic or Mr. Lukic wish to put to these witnesses who have testified matters arising from the disclosure that was made to them subsequent to the testimony, then we will arrange to have those witnesses recalled. Not in one single paragraph has Mr. Ostojic suggested that there was other questions he would have asked. Now, Your Honour, that is the simple, obvious remedy. As to whether it was a remedy that should have been required in the first place is another matter. All of these people were obvious potential Defence witnesses. I anticipate that I don't imagine we'll be told the truth about that, that these witnesses were seen by the Defence in any event. All of these matters could have been dealt with before, and if required, we will recall those witnesses. Your Honour, that is, we say, the proper remedy, not a new trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it's necessary that we discuss this issue exhaustively. Is there any response by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, if I may. I didn't use the word malice. I think it's a good word. And I think the OTP knows what it means. And it knows when it applies. The OTP may feel offended at what was said, but they certainly are not offended as officers of the Court to tell this Court the liberty of an accused is being deprived, that his rights are in jeopardy. Where was Ms. Joanna Korner when I shared with the Court that Rule 68 specifically requests three reasons why they should give us evidence. One being the credibility of witnesses. Where was Ms. Joanna Korner when I identified Witness Q who accused Slobodan Kuruzovic of crimes? Mr. Cayley and Ms. Sutherland when they were here, if we look at the transcript, they certainly told the Court. We believe in the witness's credibility. And that should be good enough. The prejudice I dare say to Ms. Korner is that Dr. Stakic's liberty is at stake. This is not a game that we can merely cure defects or flaws that occur because of what they call unintentional production of documents. We, the Defence, believe we have been reasonable. We have been tolerant. If this Trial Chamber did not specifically ask us and ask the OTP to present precise and concrete witnesses which are relevant such as other accuseds, such as other individuals who are potentially indicted, perhaps they can hide behind that mask and say "we just didn't know we were supposed to produce such documents." They knew. The OTP as a unit knew. The Decisional authority and the Chamber in Delalic and Furundzija certainly knew and warned them. Presumably they read that decisional authority. Presumably they knew that there are things such as parity between parties that is a right. That there's the equality of arms issue that other appellate decisional authority has not only discussed but mandated that we be given. But maybe each of the trial counsel here were not present when this Court discussed equality of arms. Another oversight. Call it what you will, an oversight, a misstep, or as I do in my personal and objective opinion, an intentional knowing concealment, deliberate concealment, of evidence. It is a transgression that deprived Dr. Stakic of his rights. The OTP always, since the outset, has shifted the burden to the Defence, have continuously wanted us to meet a certain level and burden of proof. They continue to do so even on this issue by stating that we should exhaustively write out the questions, exhaustively identify the witnesses, exhaustively share with the Court what other testimony witnesses should be asked. I dare say that if the OTP has reviewed our supplemental submission, we list in excess of 20 witnesses which we would like to cross-examine again, which we believe that this Chamber has a right in order to weigh their credibility and veracity. Specifically all those witnesses who were in-house that the OTP conveniently works with and brings in in each and every trial, I'd like the Court to examine the veracity of all their witnesses. We heard from Mr. Nicolas Sebire who couldn't even remember two weeks ago prior to his testimony how much time he spent in preparing tables and documents that the Court asked for and requested. On all their expert testimony, starting with their first witness, in fact, I stand corrected, starting with Ms. Joanna Korner's opening remarks where she mentioned this complicity, this conspiracy, this joint enterprise, and identifies Mr. Srdo Srdic and others on the Crisis Staff, on April 16th, 2002. Perhaps she didn't know that they had the statements and the tape recordings of the members of the Crisis Staff when she gave that opening statement. At some time, I would think, that she should have, as the rules envision, contemplated at least a simple phone call to identify those witnesses and to tell us that they have been called. The first witness Robert Donia gives a complete theory on issues such as "atmosphere of fear." He discusses the arming of Muslims and paramilitary units. Obviously based on the 30 lay witnesses that we have, that they have had for years, not giving it to the witness, may, although we might debate and doubt it, may change his opinion. But at the very least, had he reviewed that, had we had an opportunity to cross-examine Mr. Donia on that, the Court would have been better assisted in weighing his credibility. The right to a fair trial has been denied regretfully. I personally stated that we do not and will not attack the ethics or the procedural missteps of the OTP. We insist merely that they comply with the rules and that they ensure that Dr. Stakic get a fair trial which he was deprived. The prejudice is his liberty; the prejudice is the right that he had to confront and cross-examine witnesses; the prejudice is the tainting of testimony by calling in-house witnesses and giving him selective materials to review in order to give an opinion on. That is the prejudice. We have been denied all the rights that we are entitled to. That prejudice cannot be cured simply by having us write down questions so that the witness can answer them in a vacuum, whether the Court can now in hindsight recollect the witness's mannerism and credibility from this stand. That will always be something that cannot be brought back, despite Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the fact that most of their so-called in-house experts can be brought I'm sure with relative ease. It is important that the Trial Chamber heard that evidence in its proper context and not in a vacuum. We submit that it is clear not only that there have been transgressions, it is clear that the standards for a mistrial have been met, and it is unequivocally clear that Dr. Stakic suffered severe prejudice in the proceedings in light of these most recent submissions under Rule 68 given to the Defence. So we again ask respectfully of the Chamber not to weigh the economy of the issue, not to weigh the expediency of when trials should or should not be concluded, but to sincerely protect the rights of the accused and to grant us this mistrial. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Before I ask the Prosecution whether or not they have some arguments in rejoinder, I want to ask the main person in this case, and this is as I emphasised from the beginning of this case, the accused Dr. Stakic: What is his personal opinion on this request for retrial what, in fact, would mean to hear all the witnesses once again, the mere use of these first of all five to six statements we have in addition when balancing his own interests? I want to give, for reasons of fairness, the Defence the possibility to discuss this issue briefly with the client before the client may state whether or not he wants to respond to this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, as in the past, Dr. Stakic's accepts the Court's invitation and can answer the Court's question if it so wishes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Dr. Stakic, may we hear your position, balancing your own interests as indicated before.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Although I'm not too familiar with law in general, I can only state that I fully support the claims and requests made by my Defence team. What I have been able to understand from all of this is that I have suffered a great amount of prejudice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this concrete answer. May I then invite -- you may be seated please once again. May I then invite the Prosecution for, if they so want, an additional response, maybe including the question whether or not at any point in time the Prosecution intended to prepare a case against one of the six persons from which we got the six statements and whether they are preparing a case against one of these six persons in the future.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can't answer that. And it's not a question that Your Honour should require of me either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think the second -- as to the second question, that's correct. But as to the first, it might be a reason. And of course, as we did it always, we should frankly discuss these issues here. And of course the question is for the Trial Chamber why Dr. Stakic, why not one of these others?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, you came back -- and I don't think with the greatest respect it's relevant to the issue as to why Dr. Stakic and not these. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Therefore the question. Did you ever intend in the past? You have not to answer for the future. But did you ever intend in the past to indict one of these six persons?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, my recollection, and I wasn't here when all these indictments were issued, is that indictments were issued against anybody who ever moved, and some were then withdrawn. But the answer is I don't know whether they were ever to be indicted. Your Honour, but we don't rely in any event. We accept, and I want to make it absolutely clear because Mr. Ostojic seems to now be suggesting that we don't know what constitute Rule 68. We appreciate that contained in those interviews is material which potentially Rule 68. There's no question that we didn't know it. What unfortunately, and I've explained this Your Honour over and over again, and I may say I'm deeply unmoved as to whether Ostojic accepts my word or not, is that it fell through the cracks. Now the real question is, and again, Your Honour, Mr. Ostojic says the prejudice is the fact it wasn't disclosed. No, Your Honour. You have to show that in some way that information could have been used or would have been available to have cross-examined a witness in a different way and might have made a different result. The mere fact of nondisclosure in itself is insufficient. Prejudice means exactly what it says. What has the Defence not been able to do that they would have been able to do had they had this information at the relevant time? And how is it said that the use of that information may have affected the outcome of Your Honours' decision on Rule 98? Now, Your Honour, that in our submission is the real meaning of prejudice. It's not simply good enough to say "we didn't have it, so we were prejudiced." And as I said to Your Honour, the remedy is not a mistrial, but simply for the Defence to let Your Honours know and to let us know to have the witnesses recalled so they can put the questions. Now, Your Honour, I simply do not understand the reference to in-house experts such as Mr. Brown and Mr. Sebire. The Rule 68 material had nothing whatsoever to do with their evidence whatsoever. In particular, complaint was made that there was disclosure of 90 military documents when Mr. Brown began his evidence. I simply don't see -- and it's not mentioned in the motion. It's as I say the scatter-gun approach adopted by Mr. Ostojic to throw as much mud as possible and hope that some of it will stick somewhere. Your Honours, I don't think we can take this much further. As far as the witnesses are concerned, we are entitled to say this -- I'm sorry the persons we interviewed: What they had to say about things that happened conflicted with what witnesses that we were calling had to say, and we took the view not that this should be disclosed to the Defence, and as I say it fell through the cracks, but these are not witnesses upon whom the Prosecution can rely. I know that Your Honour feels that all witnesses should always -- all persons who are involved in the event should be brought before the Court, but that isn't the system. It's no more the system for the Prosecution than it is for the Defence. So Your Honour, that is the situation. But as I say, the cure, we would submit, is for the -- any witness that the Defence feels that they wish to put further matters to, to be recalled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. I have the impression that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry. I have the impression that the issue at stake has been discussed exhaustively now, and it's now for the Trial Chamber to decide. We'll see what will be the possible time frame for the decision during the break. And I think it's also necessary to have a break now. The trial stays adjourned until 4.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. The Trial Chamber is aware that the decision to be taken is an important one, on the one hand; and second, an urgent one. So we'll do our best, if possible, to decide already today. But it depends on the question whether or not we have during a longer break time enough for continuing deliberations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I just, before Your Honour moves on, correct or mention two matters that Your Honour asked me about. The two people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Arsic and Zeljaja.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. The answer is, they are thought to be in Serbia. But they're not in-- and we did issue summons and it doesn't look as though they were served. That's the best we can do. And as with Kuruzovic, Your Honour, he was summoned as a suspect. In other words, he was asked whether he wanted to have a lawyer there, so it's right to say that we were, well, the consideration has and it will be given to whether he should be indicted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification but to be on Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the safe side, let me know it is still the case that the Prosecution does not object summoning this witness by granting safe conduct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, the answer to that, Your Honour -- I think we wouldn't want to give them safe conduct because we would like to potentially arrest them. But if Your Honour wants to call them and give them safe conduct, there's not much we can do about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I asked previously I think already twice whether or not there would be objections to granting safe conduct. And at that time, the answer was always a clear yes, no objections.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, to those particular witnesses?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then, Your Honour, I'm sorry, I didn't appreciate that's been said. In this case if that has been said then I won't try and resolve from it. Your Honour, I hadn't understood that had happened. I won't resolve from that then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I only wanted come to back to Mr. Kuruzovic in special because you now mention that he was summoned as a suspect, whether this would change your attitude. But once again, do you object summoning him and at the same time granting safe conduct?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if undertakings have already been given on behalf of the OTP that we don't object, then I'm not going to object now. And I say that subject to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And this is I take it a final decision. Then leaving the question open what would be the outcome of the motion by the Defence, we have to try nevertheless to find out in case we proceed what are the witnesses. And now, the experts to be summoned. And therefore, let's come back to the so-called final witness list. I recall that in the past, the Trial Chamber already granted two expert witnesses. And it has not yet been decided by the Defence who should serve as the historian, and who should serve as the military expert as granted in the Chamber's decision dated October 8, 2002. And additionally, I recall that as regards a handwriting expert, forensic handwriting expert, we stated that a second expert on an identical issue may only be called to testify where it can be shown that he or she possesses superior knowledge, expertise, or methods of working. So this in mind, I want to ask the Defence now to concentrate first of all on these two already admitted experts. Then let's go to the handwriting expert. And then to the others. And in -- as regards now the experts, the Trial Chamber will decide in a parcel solution when having heard your submissions and, of course, the right to be heard, further submission by the Prosecution as regards the other experts. Let's start with the academic historian.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon once again, Your Honour. John Ostojic on behalf of the Defence. With respect -- we are orally requesting the Chamber to revisit and reconsider its order limiting the Defence to two experts as requested and at the time, we identified potential witnesses and potential experts we felt were necessary in order to establish the appropriate Defence for Dr. Stakic. The Court very well knows that the OTP has called in excess of two experts, despite the fact that they are in-house, to testify before the Court. We think we should not be limited to having only two experts, specifically and in light of the 98 bis order that the Court has presented to us, namely that all the counts in essence continue to survive following the OTP's case in chief. Having said that, the Defence identifies as we have orally to the OTP Srdja Trifkovic as the academic historian who will testify on behalf of the Defence. However, it should be noted that the materials, and once this report is completed, we will most certainly supply the Prosecution with the materials that Mr. Trifkovic relies upon as well as the exhibits that he relies upon, including that of who we wish to call, and that would be James Bissett. He would be having his report I believe also to rely upon. If the Defence makes a decision to call the Honourable Bissett, we will inform the parties accordingly. But at this time, our decision is that Dr. Trifkovic will be the academic historian. In addition, we would like to advise the Court that there may be some items that, like the OTP's expert witnesses, that are more of a factual nature and backdrop that Dr. Trifkovic will testify upon. As we identify in our submission to the Court, pursuant to 65 ter, he will discuss also issues ranging from this purported plan or conspiracy, the widespread and systematic attack that allegedly may have occurred. He will also discuss in detail the theory of joint criminal enterprise from a factual standpoint as well as from a historical expert standpoint.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Before I give the floor to the Prosecution, I wanted to point out and to recall that the Defence should be aware, first, that the Trial Chamber is extremely hesitant to make use of academic historians related to other issues than that what happened in the period relevant for the fourth amended indictment and the period of time immediately before. To a certain extent, coming back to and testify on the background or against the backdrop of the traumatic experiences in World War II. But it has to be limited to this area, and especially to Prijedor, and please recall that we admitted into evidence as regards Mr. Donia only this part of his testimony after long debate with the Prosecution. Second, as regards joint criminal enterprise, and this will also be true for the next expert you mentioned here in your so-called final list of witnesses all the legal questions, you mentioned joint criminal enterprise. From the legal point of view and the three categories there established in the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, the Trial Chamber will not allow an expert to discuss these issues here because the old Roman law rule applies "iudex novit curia," the judge knows the law. And therefore, we do not need legal experts. And as we also limited the Prosecution regarding historians to one only, and in this limited framework elaborated just previously, it's for the Defence to decide when you have once decided to summon Mr. Trifkovic as your academic historian, then this will be the end and no other additional historian will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just a point of clarification if I may, Your Honour, yes. If the Court recalls, many witnesses testified about the history in the region. And the OTP insisted on obtaining evidence from witnesses dealing with ARK and other matters in a general sense. We understand the Court's instruction and we appreciate it. We will keep it to a limited extent. However, there may be some instances where it's necessary to relate back, for example, when Mr. Bernard O'Donnell, another in-house expert testified, among other things, they talked about Dr. Stakic's family and they talked about World War II, that Dr. Stakic suffered items. So to keep it in context, left alone, that would unfortunately, in my opinion, hamper the Defence to say that there was some retaliation by Dr. Stakic as a result of that. That's not the case. It was presented by the OTP, although it's irrelevant. It was offered to the Court on that specific issue. But I do understand the Court's concern. We will not go back in history and revisit World War II or any other war involved in that region. We will confine our evidence primarily and specifically to that in the region of Prijedor. However, I must say that we will have to, because of the issue of joint criminal enterprise, expand and touch upon ARK to the degree but no more than the OTP has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I say that I can't see any problem with that what you just said. Already earlier, I mentioned World War II. And as far as we heard until now, it's especially related to the family of Dr. Stakic. And therefore, in the framework of what we heard from the side of the Prosecution, no doubt it has to be touched upon by your historian. And the same is true for the ARK question, because it is your intention, if I understand it correctly, to contest that what has been written down in our 98 bis decision where we, to quote from the top of my head, stated that what allegedly happened in Prijedor was allegedly embedded in a broader movement in the region related to certain other municipalities as well. So therefore, in this framework, no doubt the historian may testify. But please don't go back to the tribes in the sixth century. So this is now the historian. The military expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, but if I may, with the Court's permission, just address one other issue that the Court mentioned involving I think the constitutional law, and I think the Court mentioned that we don't want the historian to discuss the legal issues. Our historians, despite the fact that some of them may have legal backgrounds, will not discuss the law. But I would like to take the opportunity now just to address to the Court the necessity in our opinion of a constitutional expert. It is not, and if I may, Your Honour, proceed, it is not that we are calling an expert so that they can give this panel a survey of the decisional authority of this Tribunal. The allegations in the fourth amended complaint are both de facto and de jure. They are saying that the legal obligations that Dr. Stakic as president of the Crisis Staff, as president of various other bodies and institutions, had a legal obligation, whether to prevent or to stop crimes that occurred in the region. We believe, in light of the testimony and evidence presented by the OTP, there was no evidence involving de jure; yet, regretfully the count and those allegations still remain. For this panel to appreciate respectfully and understand what the legal obligations of a Crisis Staff are, what the legal obligations are of a president of a municipality in Yugoslavia, it is necessary for there to be a constitutional law expert to inform the Court of those obligations, rights, and limitations. So we are not calling an expert just so that the record is clear to assist the Court in reviewing the decisional authority here. We are calling an expert to assist the Court in determining issues that are critical and alleged against Dr. Stakic, namely on the de jure allegations, which unfortunately appear in its entirety through counts 1 through 8 of the fourth amended indictment. For the Court to understand, we would have the expert specifically talk about the local self-governing administration and government as it applied in 1992 in Prijedor relating to Dr. Stakic. But now if I may just move to the military expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We have now covered already 094, the constitutional law expert. And when we've got your -- all your submissions on these experts, then we may ask the Prosecution to give their submission as to all the experts. Military expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Our military expert is Defence witness number 91. Richard Wilmont. As identified in our 65 ter submission to the Court and the Prosecution, General Wilmont is still preparing the report and is still reviewing documents in connection with that. We expect, as I outlined specifically, that he will deal with the items on page 2 of our 65 ter submission, namely, rules of engagement during combat activities, provocation and retaliation, excessive use of force by the military, limitations and the interactions between the military and local civilian leadership. He will also discuss military hierarchy from the documents in his review. General Wilmont, we believe, will also discuss the weapons distribution. He will also in our opinion give an overview of all the documents that a military analyst should have reviewed in formulating an opinion before testifying before this Tribunal. He also has reviewed, and I can attest that he has examined the testimony, at the very least a report of Mr. Ewan Brown. He will discuss issues that are significant in the fourth amended complaint, namely those of command responsibility. He will not offer for the Court what Article 7(1), or 7(3), mandates. He will discuss from a factual basis what that purported command responsibility was as it relates to a local civilian politician. And we hope that he will survey the evidence and provide the Court with tables from my understanding, and basic outline of the evidence with respect to the military vis-a-vis the police, and then the military with respect to the local civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I ask whether the Court has anything about this general, because we have been provided with nothing at all. We understood that a military expert was a man named Hackworth. And I should point out that it's Ewan Brown, not Mr. Evan Brown.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Until now, we don't have any proffer or historic academic background.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's my understanding, Your Honour, that was submitted with the package the Court received early this afternoon. It's under Defence witness number 91, and that is what I'm reading from. I have it here if the Court would like it and obviously the Office of the Prosecution is entitled to it. We would be happy to provide it to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What I received today, it stops with 89, with number 89. And you mentioned number 91.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We'll provide the copies to the Court and the OTP at the next break. We will provide the copies, we apologise for that, to the Court and the OTP at the next break. However, that's an expert. We have been confined to having an a military expert. I'm simply informing the Court of who that is and the name of that expert. We will be glad to share that information, and as agreed with the Office of the Prosecutor, we will provide them with his complete report upon its completion.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then, Your Honour, the question I have at this stage straight away is what is the status of Mr. Hackworth or Major Hackworth or Colonel Hackworth or whatever his name is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Once again, the same applies here. The Court, balancing the interests of the parties, granted one military expert only. And I take it that when deciding in favour of General Richard Wilmont, Mr. Hackworth is no longer on the list of witnesses. Is this correct? 31.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have it. Is the Court waiting for my response on that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we believe that it's necessary in order to establish and give weight to witnesses that the Court be presented with evidence from more than just one witness, as the Prosecution has from time to time in their case presented evidence which was cumulative, repetitive. We're not asking that there be cumulative and repetitive testimony given with respect to our experts. However, we think that it is necessary since this Court will be the ultimate trier of the credibility of the witnesses, that the Defence be given an opportunity that at least two, if not three as we have envisioned and have retained as consultants, be presented so that the Court can on balance look at these differing views and make an ultimate decision based upon the evidence that was presented by the OTP's in-house expert, Ewan Brown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: As mentioned before, the Trial Chamber will rule on this later. Of course, this includes, then, all the other persons mentioned primarily as witnesses, but then it appeared that they should serve as experts. Let's turn now to the handwriting expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With respect to the handwriting expert, I have a separate comment if you will in connection with that. And I recognise and read from last week the Court's indication as well as this afternoon that there must be superior knowledge. If the Court recalls, the annex to Mr. ten Camp's report, namely the article which lists what the specific burden of proofs, if you will, are for handwriting experts, the very last sentence of that article states unequivocally that in order for any Court basically, and I'm summarising, in order for there to be an acceptance of a comparative handwriting analysis and expertise, at the very least, two experts should agree on the conclusions based upon that which they were examining and ultimately reaching a conclusion on. It's Mr. ten Camp's very own submission that there should be one other expert. We submit that Mr. James Hayes is qualified and does have superior knowledge. We will be providing the OTP hopefully later this often and no later than tomorrow afternoon a copy of Mr. Hayes' curriculum vitae. I spoke with the OTP in connection with Mr. Hayes, identified that his firm and practice were involved in many notorious cases, international, involving War Crimes Tribunal as well as notorious nationally back in the States. I believe that he does have specific superior knowledge in connection with being a handwriting comparative analyst. We hope to share with the Court what the standards and burden of proof are of various documents, how in some countries different standards are applied while in others, more stringent standards may be applied in criminal proceedings. We hope not to be cumulative or lengthy with this expert. We have not received his report yet, so I can't tell the Court definitively what it is that he will testify to. But we're confident that he will find Mr. ten Camp with respect to several of the issues consistent. And that he will not have a differing opinion. However, as Mr. ten Camp invited us in his article which is an exhibit to the Court record here, invited us and in fact instructed in my opinion that at the very least two handwriting experts be utilised in order for there to be at least some balance and understanding of whether or not the testimony should be given weight in one direction or another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Only one final question: Is it your submission that this expert will come to the conclusion that the contested signatures analysed by Mr. ten Camp are not those of Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It would be very difficult for me to say since I haven't received his report yet. But I can tell the Court what I do know is there are differing standards that the institute that certifies handwriting forensic comparative experts and comparative handwriting analysts to suggest that levels of handwriting should meet certain thresholds in criminal proceedings. That's an issue that we contested with the testimony of Mr. ten Camp, if the Court respectively recalls we felt that the standard omitted things such as beyond a reasonable doubt or most certainly two other factors. We are familiar with other standards that I think are prevalent and used throughout the world. And we would like to share that with the Court. I don't know what his conclusions will ultimately be because he's not completed his review of those documents. I anticipate, since the Defence at times had accepted some of which Mr. ten Camp said, I'm sure that there shouldn't be a dispute on those issues. But I think it's necessary, given Mr. ten Camp's very only article that he relies upon, that he uses as not only a primary source but as the main source for which comparative handwriting analysts make reference items such as no opinion or insufficient data. That it's necessary according to him to have at least two individuals in the profession agree on the topics and on the issues of signatures and authenticity of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So provisionally, we have to strike number 33 because this will serve now for the purposes of expert 97.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just add this. I'm sorry, before you move any further, we don't know what he is examining because we haven't been asked to provide any of the documents that are subject to dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'd be happy to share that with the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But in any event, Your Honour, we would object to this on the basis that the only issue is whether or not Dr. Stakic signed these particular documents, standards available in the institute of wherever it is in the United States or in Holland are irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I just wish that Ms. Joanna Korner cross-examined Mr. ten Camp so she could tell him that his standards are irrelevant. I dare say if I took that position, it would not be accepted well. I do not think they are irrelevant. Mr. ten Camp was called and requested to come here. It's his opinion that it is a necessity, and I invite the OTP to review his article, it specifically appears on the last paragraph on the annex to his report, where he himself concedes that before you can accept a handwriting expert's report, you must have at least two handwriting experts agree on any of the opinions or conclusions that are submitted. So it's his testimony that we're hoping to support, or his testimony we're hoping to enlighten the Court with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think this is a legal issue to be decided by the Tribunal. The demographer. And here, I have to recall that hopefully the Defence is aware of the limited probative value of a demographer in this case, especially related to counts 1 and 2. And -- but it's for you. What is the relevance, the necessity, to have a demographer to be heard as a Defence expert?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The Defence is unclear, respectfully, Your Honour, with respect to what the limitations are of the demographer that was offered. Again, the in-house expert, Dr. Ewa Tabeau who was offered by the OTP. We think we have an inclination. We do not want to air once again, and misunderstand the inclination that we believe exists. If Dr. Tabeau's testimony is not and will not be applied to counts 1 and 2 of the fourth amended indictment, our demographer will limit his testimony to the seventh and eighth count, namely deportation and forcible transfer. We think there is significant evidence to establish that quantitatively speaking, there cannot under the law as it exists have been or does it constitute deportation or forcible transfer from the period as alleged in the indictment. But again, the Defence is simply unclear as to the limitations that are being placed on Dr. Tabeau, and we would like, whether it be now respectfully or at a 65 ter conference, to further examine this issue and ultimately reach our decision on whether there's a necessity to call a demographer in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask who, in case you want to call a demographer, should be the demographer?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We are actually and have engaged two demographers as consultants, Your Honour. I'm not at liberty at their request to identify their names to the Court. I'm waiting for their preliminary report, expect to have the same within the next two to three weeks, and will immediately upon review of that identify the individual and provide the Court with that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I tell the Defence that the patience of the Trial Chamber is limited. The motion by the Defence is already due more than six weeks, and it takes now our time to do the work that normally should have been done by the Defence in preparation their proper 65 ter (g) motion. We don't have this motion until now in the way as foreseen in the rules. And we are not prepared to delay and delay another 65 ter conference maybe within two or three weeks. We will decide today and no later. The rules provide, however, that at the end of your case, when you feel the need and it's mandatory, we have to revisit this question. But for the purpose of the preparation of the Defence case, we should have heard witnesses the last three days of the last week and also today instead of substituting that what the Defence should have done in the past. We are no longer prepared to wait for additional informations. Number 98. Journalistic ethics.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With respect to journalists, there would be a quasi historian obviously because they would have covered the region involved in the indictment, the period. But they would also address the testimony by Mr. Vulliamy with respect to specifically the ethics involved in interviewing accused on behalf of the OTP what effect and what the role of a journalist should be in instances when they were interviewed after being asked or consulted by the OTP to go out and seek individuals such as Dr. Stakic in this case. We've identified and have three journalistic historians who can share with us the ethics involved. We believe that we will stick with David Binder on that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: That is number 7. And therefore, from the list, we can strike number 007. I don't know that this number has a special relationship to Mr. Binder. But then we know what we have to expect. We have already a short proffer on this. Then whatever this should be, under number 100. Let's be neutral, a doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, we think it's important for the Defence and the Trial Chamber to be able from a neuropsychiatrist, or a psychiatrist who we hope to have evaluate Dr. Stakic as other accuseds have in this -- in these proceedings before the Tribunal, to share with the Court and to not only mitigate but to establish for the Court some of the allegations as set forth by the OTP witnesses as well as in the fourth amended indictment; namely, these issues go, Your Honour, to the criminal mind set if you will that is alleged against Dr. Stakic, that he had a propensity and a willingness to commit and the intent, whether it's the special intent as required under count 1 of the genocide, or whether it's under count 3, the discriminatory intent under persecution. We believe that it would be helpful to the Court to have an appreciation and understanding of what a neuropsychiatrist would be able to share with the Court, especially in light of the fact that Dr. Stakic's family history has been brought and presented in as evidence, namely, the item that we discussed earlier involving World War II and his grandfather, et cetera. We, unfortunately, and we accept the Court's view with respect to perhaps the tardiness of the Defence. But pursuant to Rule 65 ter, we believe if the Court looks, and we know you have, so I say it with most respect, at (g), and specifically (i), the sub-paragraphs request that we give the name or pseudonym of each witness, and we give a summary of the facts. I recognise that it's important for the preparation of the -- for the OTP to prepare. We will give them, I assure the Court, more time than they have ever given us for any of the witnesses. We will not introduce documents during the testimony, on the eve of testimony, or even after their testimony as they have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask, what are the concrete facts on which such an expert witness will testify? Is it your submission that you are afraid that in the past, anybody, be it a witness or be it the Prosecution or the Chamber, indicated that there would be the slightest indication that Dr. Stakic would suffer from any disease leading to the result that there would be a limited or total non-culpability?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I am not a physician or a neuropsychiatrist. If that's the case, it will be presented us. Unfortunately, the issues that a neuropsychiatrist will evaluate and help us understand is whether there's this propensity as alleged by the OTP of this special intent or discriminatory intent or any type of hatred by Dr. Stakic to another human being much less than as it is alleged in the fourth amended indictment. I think it's necessary for the Defence to be given that opportunity. And secondly, if I may, with all due respect, since the Court limited us to two experts at the prior occasion we hesitated to spend funds that we do not have as does the OTP to call this neuropsychiatrist and to have him evaluate Dr. Stakic prior to the Court's authorisation. We believe that such an evaluation can be done in short order, and the report can be tendered to the Court rather quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What would be the name of this expert witness following 65 ter (g) (i) (a)?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm trying off the top of my head the name of the expert that we would utilise. There are two which have as the Court indicated superior knowledge. I want to say the name of Dr. Russler, with an R. But I can't be certain, Your Honour. And again forgive me for not being certain. We identified this category with the intent to seek leave of court to be able to retain that neuropsychiatrist to evaluate Dr. Stakic as well as the other experts who we've identified only by category.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do we agree that at this point in time, this medical expert be stroken [sic] from the list of experts?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I may, so long as it's without prejudice and with leave to resubmit and ask the Court at a later time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We object, Your Honour. There's not the slightest bit of evidence ever been led in this case that Stakic is suffering from any sort of mental problems, that he is in any way suffering from diminished responsibility for his actions, and all a psychiatrist can tell you is what Dr. Stakic said to him today ten years after the event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think that when we agree that any kind of medical expert is no longer on the list, it may be cured if necessary under Rule 73 ter (F) that Trial Chamber may grant Defence request for additional time to present evidence if this is in the interest of justice. But as to the fact that we agreed for this point in time that there is no necessity, we strike the neuropsychiatrist. The police expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We believe that a police expert is necessary for the Defence to establish for the Court items that are core and critical to the fourth amended indictment. As the Court sees, reading or a cursory review of the indictment, there are specific allegations that various members of the police, members of the reserve police, members of an organisation that may have been considered a paramilitary police, were involved in some atrocities in the region. It is necessary for, we believe, the Court to have an appreciation of the police hierarchy and structure in Prijedor in 1992. What that relationship was with respect to the military, what that relationship was as it may relate to the civilian authorities, this goes to the heart of the issue under article 7(3) namely command superior responsibility. The Court will recall that the indictment against Dr. Stakic was sealed and secret two days prior to his arrest. The Court will also recall that in the indictment, a police chief by the name of the late Simo Drljaca had been indicted, had been killed. It is as a result of that that we believe a police expert is necessary in order for the Defence to establish and elaborate upon the elements specific in the fourth amended indictment. We are prepared to share with the Court the name of the police expert if the Court so wishes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I'm more than surprised to hear this last sentence. I think it's clear in a way that it can't be more clear in 65 ter (g) (i) (a), that you have first of all - and this is the absolute minimum - to provide a name.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'd like to address that point specifically. The Defence will not be treated differently than the OTP. If the Court recalls, the OTP in their 65 ter submission identified exactly category similar to these without giving us the name, the curriculum vitae, or the basis of the testimony. They shared that information with us when it deigned on them to give it to us, when the reports were complete, when they were able to fashion the testimony in the manner which they so desired. The reason we do not identify the expert on our witness list is because we do not want to go against Court's prior ruling which limited us to two experts. We cannot and will not identify the witnesses if the Court told us you're limited to two. We've restated the categories because we would like the Court to reconsider those issues. We are prepared to identify that expert. And I will share it with the Court. His name is Dr. Dusko Vanovic -- Vejnovic. Vejnovic. V-E-J-N-O-V-I-C. First name Dusko, I believe. And he's a Ph.D.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So finally, before I invite the OTP for the summary, the one remains on the list. This is forensic criminal analyst, whatever this shall be.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Typically, a forensic criminal analyst, from my recollection, and I believe when I used the name of Dr. Russler with an "R" I think that was actually the name of the forensic criminal expert. He can identify criminal behaviour from individuals and would be able to share with the Court whether there's a propensity for such behaviour. utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
