utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. As you may have seen from the mere fact that it took the Chamber several days to decide on the motion on mistrial and the remaining point was only point 1 of this decision, we thought -- we believe that we have before us a serious violation of Rule 68. We had to visit, revisit, the jurisprudence by this Tribunal from Furundzija, Celebici, and the last one was I think in Simic on these omissions by the Prosecution under Rule 68. I think in this case it is not disputed that there was such a violation of Rule 68. It is not for the Trial Chamber to find out what are the underlying reasons, whether there was negligence, cross-negligence, or as alleged by the Defence, even deliberate infringement of Rule 68. In Brady 373, United States at 87, it was held "that the suppression by the Prosecution is evidence favourable to an accused upon request violates due process where the evidence is material either to guilt or to punishment, irrespective of the good faith or bad faith of the Prosecution." So it's -- from this it's quite clear that it is the right to have access to this material under Rule 68 as soon as possible and as soon as practicable for the Defence. And it is also necessary for the Trial Chamber, because how should we, the Judges, exercise our mandate if we don't have the facts? And only when we have the facts, we can decide. And we are mandated to come as close as possible to the truth as we can find it in the rules governing the ethics of the Defence where we can read, in the standards of professional conduct for Prosecution counsel, it is to assist the Tribunal to arrive at the truth and to do justice for the international community, victims, and the accused. How can we find out and how can we decide under Rule 98, sentence 2, or 85 (v) if we don't know that these statements exist as we have before us now? The question arising, however, is is there any violation of due process or the principle of fair trial. And this is, first of all, a question of the materiality of the evidence. In Bagley 473, United States, at 678, it is said that "Bagley's touchstone of materiality is a reasonable probability of a different result, and the adjective is important. The question is not whether the defendant would more likely than not have received a different verdict with the evidence, but whether in it's absence he received a fair trial, understood as a trial resulting in a verdict worthy of confidence. The reasonable probability of a different result is accordingly shown where the government's evidentiary suppression undermines confidence in the outcome of the trial." Already from this it follows that a high threshold is applicable. And this is also the case here when deciding on the motion before us. We are aware that the statements contain, in fact, ambiguous material. And we came to the conclusion that we can exclude that the final outcome of the case is not affected. And this is the test used, for example, in the United States and especially there Brady. The outcome is as said not affected because of the ambiguity, the final outcome. An additional question was raised by the Defence: What about our 98 bis decision? Was there any impact on this decision by the omission of the OTP which could result in a restoration of the status quo ante. We, especially the Judges, having signed the 98 bis motion, when conscientiously going through the statements, we came to the conclusion that having decided as mentioned before unanimously, therefore, not needing to contact Judge Fassi Fihri, we can conscientiously state that the outcome, the result, would have been the same if we would have had these statements before us already earlier. Then it comes down to the final question: Is there any prejudice, and especially is there prejudice that can't be cured? And here, we came to the conclusion that, no doubt, the Defence has the possibility to call these witnesses during their case. And whenever they want, they may request the reappearance of witnesses, but already at this point in time, we have to emphasise that it would be for the Defence to demonstrate on the basis of concrete questions that the Defence was not able to put these concrete questions to the witnesses when they had been here in The Hague, and that these new questions are emanating from the statements missing at that point in time. Therefore, in result, we come to the conclusion that there was no prejudice for the accused, that it does not affect the final outcome of the case. And therefore, the principles of due process and fair trial are not infringed. The motion is, therefore, rejected. It's not rejected without a stern warning in the direction of the Office of the Prosecution to fulfill their obligations under Rule 68 forthwith. This principle has to be applied by the test in doubt to disclose the material obtained by the Prosecution when in doubt it tends, as we can read it from Rule 68, to be exculpatory material. Only this enables in future the Defence to exercise their obligations and at the same time it enables only this enables the Trial Chamber to exercise their obligations under Rule 98 bis and 95 (v) [sic]. Then let me turn to the question of experts. In conclusion, I can already state now that we stick to our earlier decision on 65 ter -- on expert witnesses. Why this? We admitted an historian, here number 87, Mr. Trifkovic, and we admitted a military expert, General Richard Wilmont. It's, first of all, balancing the interests of both parties and the fact that also the Prosecution, in fact, provided us with the testimony of such witnesses, expert witnesses. But we did not see, and it was not demonstrated, that there was any necessity to hear a second military expert, Mr. Richard [sic] Hackworth. Therefore, we strike this witness from the list of witnesses. Constitutional law expert, I think it's the mandate - and we already stated this earlier - it's the competence and the mandate of this Trial Chamber to decide on these legal questions, summarising the contribution by the Defence counsel, it comes down to the question whether or not 7(3) of our Statute was part of customary international law already in 1992 and whether or not it would amount to apply laws of substantive criminal law retroactively. This is a question that can only be decided by the Trial Chamber. As regards the handwriting expert, we stated in our earlier decision what is the threshold to admit a second handwriting expert. And we found that it is not correct that what was submitted by the Defence that Mr. ten Camp requested or recommended to have a second expert handwriting -- handwriting expert. Of course, he stated that there are different international standards that could be applicable, and therefore the outcome, the parameters of the decision, could be different, applying different national standards. But we don't know anything about, and it was not demonstrated, that Mr. Hayes would have superior knowledge or possibilities or scientific methods not available for Mr. ten Camp. Therefore, also, we have to strike also Mr. Hayes from the list of witnesses. As regards an expert on journalistic ethics, we don't see that this can be regarded as an expert. It is another approach how to conduct journalistic research, but it is for the Trial Chamber to find out whether, for example, in this case Mr. Vulliamy is reliable evidence, is credible. And it's not -- it can't be countered by another journalist, especially when this journalist has never been and we never found any submission related to this, has never been in Prijedor. By striking David Binder from the list of witnesses, we had to come back and revisit witness number 51, Peter Maher. But the same is true as what was said related to David Binder. Also he has never visited Prijedor, never had contacted Dr. Stakic. And therefore, it would amount to the testimony of another journalist. But the relevance of this testimony has not been demonstrated. Finally, the police expert. Once again, the relevance of this testimony has not been demonstrated. It was the Defence counsel's submission that it wouldn't be necessary to provide more under 65 ter, or, in addition, that when ruling earlier on the question of experts and on the admission of experts, they didn't expect that any additional expert witness would be admitted. This is not correct. As you can read it from the transcript, we invited explicitly in our order the Defence, if need may be, to demonstrate the relevance of these experts. And this is necessary not only under 65 ter (g), but 65 ter (g) has always to be read together with Rule 73 (c) because here it's the obligation for the Trial Chamber to find out whether or not the -- a witness has to be heard or - let me quote - "in the light of the file submitted to the Trial Chamber by the pre-trial judge, pursuant to Rule 65 ter (l) (ii), the Trial Chamber, after having heard the Defence, shall set the number of witnesses the Defence may call." And the same is true without any doubt for expert witnesses. Finally, I didn't mention until now Professor Robert Hayden, professor of anthropology. Once again, we couldn't identify the relevance in the summary of the testimony, of the expected testimony. The Office of the Prosecution did not consent under Rule 92 bis. And in fact, the first -- already in the first sentence, the submission by the Defence, is that this witness should testify and it would be relevant, his testimony, on widespread and systematic campaign. Once again, one element of crime that has to be assessed by the Trial Chamber and nobody else. Finally, it was for the Trial Chamber to decide under Rule 65 ter (n). There it reads: "The Trial Chamber shall decide should the case arise on sanctions to be imposed on a party which fails to perform its obligations pursuant to the present rule. Such sanctions may include the exclusion of testimonial or documentary evidence." We are of the opinion that especially related to the latter sanction, there would be prejudice for Dr. Stakic. And already from this point of view, we can't take into account this sanction. The other sanction mentioned in an order of this Trial Chamber earlier was the question of whether or not it was adequate in this concrete consolation to ask the Registrar to redact a certain portion of the fees related to these motions from the Defence. Once again, the Trial Chamber found that this would be not an appropriate reaction. And I want to leave with this: Especially balancing the omissions of both parties and this possibility is only available in one direction, therefore, in conclusion, we decided not to impose any sanctions under Rule 65 ter (n). But once again, we have to alert the Defence and recall their ongoing duty to cooperate as foreseen under Rule 65 ter (g) in order to avoid any other undue delay as we had it during the last days. This concludes today's hearing. The trial stays adjourned until Monday, 9 December, 14.15 in this courtroom.
